utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Robinson is absent due to Tribunal business, so we'll sit pursuant to 15 bis. Mr. Milosevic, for you to continue examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon. Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Gojovic. Yesterday, we went through tab 14 containing a number of documents from which it transpires that you as the head of the general administration of the General Staff were informed about the work of the courts and the prosecutors' offices. Was the Supreme Command Staff informed of the work of the military judiciary organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to draw everyone's attention to tab 15. It contains a paper titled "Information." Was that the kind of information that was supplied to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the kind of report we received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It contains all the general data about formation, 1st Army, 2nd Army, 3rd Army. In the penultimate paragraph, concerning the 3rd Army, it says: "The difficulties encountered by this court in its work also exist when it comes to delivering subpoenas because of the lack of security and safety of movement in combat operations zones, the intense attacks carried out by the aggressor's air force and the covert operations by dispersed terrorists groups."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is typical of the military corps and the military prosecutor's office of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps, in fact its zone of responsibility covers the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Is that correct, General Gojovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the next page, in paragraph 3, we see information about the number of cases. It says: "From the moment of establishment of military judicial organs, military prosecutors received 7.807 criminal reports, filed reports for the investigation of 2.911 persons, and charged 3.928 persons. A total of 2.825 requests to start an investigation were submitted. 1.395 were implemented. Some 3.897 persons have been indicted ..." That is the kind of information you showed us in the form of tables.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to give a clarification about this. This paper was prepared for over a number of days, and it's dated 12th September, but this information is as of the 15th September, because that was the date when we actually submitted it to the Supreme Command Staff, and the information was updated before it was sent. There were certain corrections to these conclusions and assessments. So these numbers - for instance the number of cases - coincides with the numbers given in tabular form in the tables we saw earlier in attachments annexes 1 to 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The basic problems are also covered here. In paragraph 4, it says: "A large number of criminal reports were submitted in a very short interval, and many of them were not supported by the necessary legal evidence, which causes difficulties in the work of the prosecutor. Such a large number of criminal cases are becoming a burden to the courts. "There is a slight increase in more -- in graver, serious crimes, with an increasing number of perpetrators committing serious crimes, which represents a threat to society and requires greater engagement of the competent organs in order to detect and prevent crimes."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, we see what kind of measures were applied. It says: "Provide adequate documentation for establishment of military prisons," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request for the accused to provide adequate references before starting to quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are being requested by the interpreters to indicate the appropriate references before starting to quote.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 6.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "All commanders of units should report immediately to the military prosecutor any crimes and perpetrators so that they can be prosecuted. Any officers who do not comply shall be accountable and the strictest measures shall be applied against them." That's the kind of information that was supplied to the Supreme Command Staff. This is dated 12 September 1992. Do you have any comments, Mr. Gojovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is especially this paragraph concerning the work of the courts where they are urged to do their utmost so that all these cases can be processed in the most efficient manner. The date of this document is 12 May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we might have a little bit more information about this document. The witness has been asked whether it's like material he received. I don't know if he's saying he received it or where he got it from or how he produced it, but given that it's anonymous on its face, perhaps a little more detail will help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Nice can deal with it in cross-examination, but if you can help us with this question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can deal with it. I personally drafted this paper. All the reports that went to the Supreme Command Staff regarding the work of the military judiciary bodies were personally drafted by me. Some corrections and adjustments were introduced here by my superior, General Matovic, concerning the work of the Supreme Command Staff. Otherwise, I compiled all this data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is indicated here that it was the administration for reinforcement, organisation, mobilisation, and system issues of the Supreme Command Staff drafted this.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. The legal department of the Supreme Command Staff was part of this administration, and I drafted this with the approval of the head of this administration, General Matovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says "attachments as indicated in the text." Those are the attachments we reviewed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and those attachments contain exact data on cases processed. So this is a package of documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me in the most general terms what issues from the domain of the work of military judiciary were reported to the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were reported about the number of perpetrators, the number of criminal reports received, the number of requests for starting investigations, and the number of indictments. As for military courts, how many on-site investigations were carried out, how many requests for investigations were received, how many investigations were actually started, how many indictments were brought. Also, the Supreme Command Staff was given a breakdown by the type of crimes. There were three types of crimes concerning military courts; failure to respond to call-up, desertion, and failure to carry out orders. All other crimes were put in one group. There is crime against life and limb, that is murder; heavy bodily injuries; and the third category is crimes against property. Crimes against property, as I said, they encompass all crimes concerning property. Additional information would be later submitted concerning the status of persons who committed the crimes; officers, non-commissioned officers, conscripts, et cetera. That is the kind of issues that were contained in the reports given to the Supreme Command Staff, including tables where all this data is contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, can I take it that crime against life and limb includes more than murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All crimes against life and limb are crimes against life and body, in other words. There is nothing else in this category.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, did the Supreme Command Staff, after the state of war ended, receive a final report of all criminal cases started before military judiciary organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the document contained in tab 16, "Report on the work of military judicial organs during the state of war"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again can I be clear about one thing: The last document we've looked at, which is tab 15, is dated at the end a date in May, 12th of May, but at the beginning a date in September. Now, what period does it actually relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. It was not September. I'm sorry. The previous report provides information as of the 12th of May, but it is accompanied by annexes added as of the 15th of May, and the information is added, as I explained earlier, speaking of para 3, that the information was updated before the report was finally submitted. The report took two or three days to compile, and we updated it before submitting it on the 15th, because this report was submitted together with the tables we discussed previously, and we updated the information so that all the data would coincide between the tables and the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have that tab 15 with you, General Gojovic? What Judge Bonomy has referred to is a handwritten date on the right top of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the 12th of May. 12th of May. I wrote that in longhand so I wouldn't have to turn to the last page and look at the date, the last page in the left-hand corner. This is written in pencil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the first page, at the top of the right part of the page, it says 12th of September, 1999. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's the 12th of May. 12/9 -- 12/5. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's a misinterpretation. Yes, I follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Must be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One problem about that is a number of your answers have actually referred to September, but we can take it that they're wrong, can we, and they should be May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the month of May. Maybe it was a slip of the tongue. Maybe President Milosevic can help us, but I kept speaking of the 12th of May. I kept speaking of the month of May, not September. It must be a misunderstanding or misinterpretation. In any case, it's the month of May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have the original of that document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what can you see on that document, the original? Can you see -- can we see what you wrote down in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Take a look, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the copy isn't clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's clear, yes. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I'd like to tender tab 15 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit from tab 13 and 14 and 15 as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already answered my question, that is to say whether the staff of the Supreme Command received a final report at the end of the state of war, which means also at the end of the existence of wartime courts; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're just going to dwell on this very briefly. On page 1, paragraph 3, we see the total figure that: "Military prosecutors have so far received a total of 18.541 criminal reports, filed requests for the investigation of 5.370 persons, and indicted 6.708 persons." Can you explain to us how an investigation was conducted against 5.370 whereas 6.708 were indicted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the situation when you have a cross-section like this. Part of the persons were accused after the investigation, and the second portion were individuals which were not investigated if the evidence and proof was sufficient, together with the criminal file -- criminal report that was filed, for the prosecutor to be able to go ahead in the proceedings, and this was something we could do during a situation of war, which means that without the acquiescence of the investigating judge, an indictment could be raised whereas regularly you would need agreement from the investigating judge to raise an indictment for serious crimes meriting sentences above five years. So that is the difference. It was a state of war and that's why that difference occurs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I've understood your explanation. The third paragraph from the bottom on that same first page says the following, that sentences ranged "from one to seven years in prison, with the majority being around 2.5 to six years, while for other serious crimes, far more severe sentences were pronounced."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was for the cases where a judgement was made, and there were fewer people where the high sentences existed, there were -- the cases were referred on appeal. Towards the end of this piece of information, it says crimes which -- criminal cases that will objectively not be able to be completed will be sent to the responsible peacetime military courts for further procedure as envisaged by the rules of operation of military courts during a state of war."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this absolutely in keeping with the rules of service and rules of procedure, that wartime military courts are abolished and regular courts of law carry on with the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once the state of war ceases, the military judiciary ceases to work, which means that we don't need extra regulations for this. Once a state of war has come to an end, so do the military courts, and it is the peacetime military courts that take over these affairs. In Nis, in Belgrade or Podgorica. So there were three military courts during peacetime covering the entire area and the area of Kosovo and Metohija for the 3rd Army. All the cases are ceded to the military court in Nis. The 1st Army has its military court in Belgrade, and the 2nd Army has its military court in Podgorica and they continue to work regularly in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we, General, now comment briefly on the attachments to this piece of information, the state of criminal cases in military judicial organs, the table we have, and criminal reports received against officers 172, 107 against non-commissioned officers, 3.843 against privates, private soldiers, 14.252 against military conscripts, 31 against civilians in the Yugoslav army, and 136 criminal reports received against civilians not in the Yugoslav army, which makes a total of 18.541.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This gives us the total number of criminal reports broken up according to the categories of persons committing the crimes, and this is important for the supreme military staff to see who the perpetrators were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. according to the criminal reports filed and received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And next -- in the last column we see investigation requests, how many indictees, what the judgements were. The total number is 2.185, 360 were freed, which makes a total of 2.811 judgements during the state of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was while the bombing was going on, to all intents --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the time a state of war was declared until it was -- it came to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have on the next page convictions by category of persons. Could you just tell us briefly about the column referring to crimes against life and limb.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convicted persons for crimes against life and limb that the president has just referred to shows the following: The total number of convicted persons is 2.811, and they are divided up in categories, categories of crimes and the sentences passed, from the smallest sentence to the longest prison sentence. But as I said, 32 is the total number for that category, up to 2 years, 28; up to five years, 4 persons. Four persons received sentences of up to 5. So those are the judgements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the others are the ones where proceedings continue.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the last column shows the total number of convicted persons. 2.185 convicted, 360 acquitted, and dismissed 266. This dismissal - let me just explain this to you. The difference between acquitted and dismissed is that when the prosecutor gives up during the main investigations, gives up the case where he feels there's no case to answer. Where there is not sufficient proof and evidence to raise an indictment, then the case is dismissed. And this is distinguished from the acquittals column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just take note of that. All the convicted persons, including the most serious crimes, were convicted during the state of war or, rather, during the bombing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the courts dislocated, that they moved, that they would have to go into safer areas because they were the target of the bombing. Now, you yourself, based on your personal experience, did you encounter a situation where you had to move?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I took up my duties on the 16th of April. From the 16th of April to the 10th of June, we had to dislocate three times, move three times, and before that they had to move twice, which means a total of five dislocations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can I have some clarification from you on what the issue is that this evidence relates to, this evidence of the general judicial system that was in operation at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, this relates to the main charges in the indictment according to which it is said that the forces of Yugoslavia or Yugoslav army perpetrated crimes in Kosovo and Metohija, whereas on the basis of all this, we can see - of course nobody questions or challenges the fact that there were crimes that had been committed - but we can see from this material the whole chain of command and the judiciary, the court organs that were working to punish the crimes that were committed, to bring the perpetrators to justice, and to bring them to court, to take them into custody and to try them. And the executive powers say that perpetrators of crimes must be brought before the court. Once they are in court, it goes -- they come under the domain of court authorities, the judiciary, and not executive power and authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But would the perpetrators that really matter in this case not all be dealt with by the military court and, therefore, should we not be looking at the cases that the military court dealt with and perhaps the detail of these cases rather than the general cases of ordinary criminal activity in the country?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand it, these are just cases that were dealt with by the military court and military prosecutor's office. The cases that went to civilian courts and the civilian prosecutor's office are not incorporated into these documents, nor does General Gojovic, in view of his military functions, is able to testify about what civilian courts did. So these are cases before the military courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're quite right, but what I'm really getting at is that the only category presumably that really matters here is the crimes against life and limb. The desertion or the failure to answer your conscription call-up and so on is neither here nor there. What we really must be interested in is damage to life and limb and possibly damage to property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And whether it is a crime against humanity or a war crime.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to crimes against life and limb, without a doubt in most cases that's what we did deal with. That's what these cases are. I can't -- the majority. And I can't say that all of them were, but General Gojovic is here to explain that. Whereas the tables were provided as they exist in the documents and as the documents sent up to the higher authorities, that is to say to General Gojovic himself and how he informed the Supreme Command. We didn't make extracts and excerpts from those documents, but as you can see, I'm asking General Gojovic about crimes against life and limb. And I should like to mention in this regard that General Gojovic yesterday indicated that the military prosecutors were guided in their work by the practice of giving more serious sentences --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Bringing in graver charges, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for these crimes. And some of these crimes even merited the death sentence whereas the Criminal Code in Yugoslavia had no death sentence provisions or, rather, didn't have at that time, and now it doesn't exist in the Criminal Code of Serbia either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might I be allowed to give an explanation, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not at the moment, please. I just want to make it clear, Mr. Milosevic, that for my part this evidence would be more significant if we were looking at examples to see what is the nature of the case that's being taken up by the military court that might be a case that was an example of criminal activity that would fall under the terms of the indictment, and I don't really at the moment have any idea of what these cases were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I hope that by the end of my examination-in-chief of General Gojovic you will get an idea of what this is about, because the descriptions of the cases that we're dealing with will be found in the tabs to come. We haven't come to that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are looking forward to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Gojovic, please put a pause between the question and answer, for the sake of the interpreters. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, I think you wanted to give an additional explanation in this regard.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I wanted to indicate this - not to waste time - what I wanted to say was that we are going to see the individual cases next individually and the way and what crimes were committed and which crimes come under war crimes or crimes against international humanitarian law. So you will have the names and surnames, the events, and the judgement of the court in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, I know that because I've read through the documents. I'm just anxious to try to make some progress.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to try and move ahead as quickly as possible, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, are the military -- is the military judiciously independent in its work?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course certainly. Without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Supreme Command or any other level of command in the army of Yugoslavia, did it have the right to influence the work of the military judiciary in any way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command was not able to exert influence on the work of the courts on the individual cases except to provide necessary working conditions and to insist upon speeding up the whole process. So if you can consider that to be an influence, then in that way, but as -- as to the method of decision-making, that came under the jurisdiction of the prosecutor in the first place and the military courts and nobody was allowed to meddle or interfere in their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when we come to the chain of command, could you explain to us, if an officer learns or suspects that a crime has been committed, what must he do? What is his duty?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every officer is duty-bound to act in one of the following ways, or in the following ways: First of all, if it is in his -- if his -- the crime is committed on the territory of his unit, he must secure the area, safeguard the evidence, take measures to uncover the perpetrators, to prevent them from absconding. So those are the first steps. Then he is duty-bound to inform the military prosecutor or, rather, the organs of the military police for them to take further steps to apprehend the perpetrator. And if he does all this, then he is duty-bound to file a criminal report to the military courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now, where does the -- where do the duties of the officer end?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the officer has filed a criminal report, gathered all the evidence, then it is the prosecutor who takes over. Where an investigation is necessary and where the search for the perpetrator has to be undertaken, then that is left to the military police and then the duties of the officer cease. It is the professional organs that come into play at that second stage to uncover the perpetrator and to gather evidence. So those are the first steps that the officer takes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the French booth and Albanian booth do not have the document, so could you slow down. And the last part was not interpreted. Could you repeat the last question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said to the witness that I wished to move on to tabs 17 and 18, and the question is:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the crimes committed that could be considered grave violations of international humanitarian law whose perpetrators were discovered and for whom proceedings were initiated before courts of law during the state of war? I'm referring to tab 17. This is a letter sent to the supreme military court in Belgrade. It deals with the period from the 24th of March, 1999, to the 10th of June, 1999, that is to say when the NATO aggression started. Could we please go through tab 17 now. I would just like you to indicate -- or, rather, we have all the tables here of all the crimes involved in the period from the 24th of March until the 10th of June, so this involves a great deal of statistics. That's why I asked for tab 17, where we have a summary review of criminal proceedings instituted against persons who committed crimes in the area of Kosovo and Metohija during the NATO aggression, that is to say from the 24th of March until the 10th of June, 1999. General Gojovic, if we look at the contents, we can see -- well, actually, I'm going to skip over the summary review. Item 2 is war crimes against the civilian population. This is on pages 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three are multiple murders and you mentioned the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia from pages 4 to 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you indicate the page number in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got the English version now, but it's always just a couple of pages. I mean in the English version too item 2 has to start on page 2, because the first page is the summary review.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have here war crimes against the civilian population. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I couldn't find the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please get this tab in English, and then I'll be able to find the reference for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it tab 18, then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, tab 18. As soon as you go through the contents, I assume there would have to be something that says "Summary," and then there's this summary review of one page only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the problem is we were referred to tab 17. But is it 18?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Tab 17 are simply all the statistical surveys, but then tab 18 is concrete. That is what you insisted on, Mr. Bonomy. In the English text, it starts from page 4, Mr. Kwon. Page 4, war crimes against the civilian population. In the English text it is page 4, in the Serbian text it is page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think we are following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it says here Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then the name and surname of the accused person, the time of commission of crime, the place of commission. It's the Istok municipality, you can see it here. As you can see on this first page -- or, rather, the page that is page number 4 in the English language, five persons were indicted, and then there is a brief description of crime. That's what it says in English, too, "Brief description of crime." And then the persons are mentioned, and it says they "killed with premeditation five unidentified Albanians whom they had previously taken prisoner and detained during an operation by their unit. Having taken them out of custody, they put them against the wall of a house, opened fire on them with automatic rifles and killed them all. They threw them into a well into which they poured petrol and then set it on fire." Those proceedings or, rather, that case was later referred to the court in Kraljevo. It has to do with five individuals. All five are reserve soldiers. And then A is Istok municipality and B is Donja Klina municipality. These same persons removed two Albanians from a refugee convoy in Donja Klina, they opened fire on them with automatic rifles in the yard of an abandoned house, killed them, and then threw them into a well. In the English text this is page number 5. On that same page, page number 5, there is an indicted captain first class reserve, and the description of the crime reads as follows: "As platoon commander, he order his subordinate soldiers to fire at a Siptar in a meadow in order to check the adjustments on their weapon sights. In so doing, they killed him. He also ordered them to take money, gold jewellery, and other valuables from the Siptar population." Later on, the case was referred to the district court in Valjevo. On page 6 in the English version - and in the Serbian language it's on page 4 - there are three persons. There is a major, there is a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reserve private, and yet another reserve private. It says here that this officer, in the Susica village sector where his unit was, he ordered the two privates to liquidate Feriz Krasniqi and Rukija, an elderly man and woman who had not left the village. They did not -- they did this, shooting at them with their automatic rifles. Further on on the same page, there are three persons and there is a description of the crime concerned. On the same page, there is a crime committed by a reserve private. This is number 4. It says: "In the Penduh village sector where a convoy of military vehicles had stopped, when he saw two people, Flazmin Emini and Bahri Emini, running away, he discharged a burst of gunfire after them from an automatic rifle and killed both of them." However, I think it would be better if the general could make comments with regard to all of this rather than have me read it out. The next page is page 7 in the English version, numbers 5, 6, 7 respectively. He killed Kaljif Berisa and Saljiju Pucoli, two Roma from Kosovo Polje using an automatic rifle. Then the next person under number 6 is reserve captain first class, a particular captain. "Having taken five people from the village of Zagradska Hoca into custody, he lined them up against a wall and then killed one of them with one round from his rifle and the others with a burst of fire. And then soldier Igor Radojica, who killed several people, and so on and so forth. All of that is on page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask something, Mr. Milosevic? I would like to ask two things, actually. One is in this catalogue, this list of cases where people were prosecuted or proceedings were taken up in relation to what might be described as war crimes, are any of these cases referred to in the indictment? In other words, are any of them cases that the Prosecution have taken up with the allegation that they are a war crime or are these all quite separate cases that were individually prosecuted in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Bonomy, that this is perfectly clear evidence that the organs of the army of Yugoslavia, the judiciary of the military of Yugoslavia, arrested people, brought them to courts of law, and submitted criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. That's not my question. My question is whether any of them, any of them appear in the indictment. It's just to try and relate these events to see if they're entirely separate events from the ones that the Prosecution are dealing with or if there's any coincidence between the cases here and the particular crimes that are alleged in the indictments. I'm only looking for some assistance to make the job easier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. Bonomy, but it is my understanding that Mr. Nice is dealing with all victims for whom he believes were killed by Serb soldiers and officers, by the forces of Serbia and Yugoslavia. So this refers to such victims, with the names and surnames of the perpetrators who were discovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Many victims are named in the indictment, and I just wondered if any of those named in the indictment against you appear in this catalogue of cases which were taken up by the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you that I did not compare the lists that appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice has the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour may be assisted on page 76.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 76, Izbica. Izbica is charged. Although, of course, I'm waiting to hear what the witness has to say about this as about other entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean 76 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, sorry, page 76 of this exhibit. Page 76 of this exhibit, as I have it, in English is unknown persons, Izbica village, near Srbica. Now that, I think, may relate to something that's charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the indictment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the only one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as we've seen so far. We've only had the translations since yesterday. That's the best we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful. The second matter I wanted to raise was directly with the general. Can you explain to me how this document was compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. The survey we are looking at now is one that I personally compiled on the basis of the original documents from the Nis military court. This is a report that was sent to the supreme military court in Belgrade. This comes from the documents of the Nis military court. They dealt with things in order, in chronological order as they were entered in their register. I made this survey, and I tried to group the crimes so they could be followed more easily. You will see the page number reference and the type of crime committed in order to be able to follow things more easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was done in 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry. But the information contained therein goes up to the 10th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to go back to the very beginning now, but it's page 8. I want to draw your attention to the fact that all the columns are the same, and there is also ruling to initiate proceedings. And if you look at your page 8, and you will see that for the person under number 1, the rule to initiate proceedings was -- ruling to initiate proceedings bears the date of the 25th of April, 1999, and for the other person the date is May 1999. So could you please just explain, General, criminal reports have to be filed, I assume, before this ruling or decision is made to initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is done by the investigating judge. Once he receives this request and once he interrogates the suspect, he decides whether he is going to initiate proceedings or not. According to the law on criminal procedure, it is only then that proceedings actually start before a court of law. Before that, it is in the hands of the prosecutor's office, and that is not part of court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very important to state that all these preliminary dates have to precede the date when the decision is made to initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We can move on further. On page 7, or, rather, in the English translation it is page 9. There are four numbers yet again. Under number 1 we see again murder. A soldier fired a burst of fire from his automatic rifle at Rusiti Rusiti, inflicting injuries on him and his wife. We see the decision to start criminal proceedings 26 of May 1999. Number 2 and number 3. At the time when their unit was in the general sector of Pec, they opened fire on an Albanian for no reason, without provocation, and killed him. Under number 4, another private reserve discharged a burst of fire from his automatic rifle at a Siptar, hit him, and inflicted fatal injuries. Proceedings -- ruling to initiate proceedings is dated 4th of May, 1999. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you established sufficient foundation to exhibit this document. I don't think you have to read out all the items. But I'm interested in knowing about the future conviction. How were they dealt with by the courts referred to? Are you going to introduce that evidence in the future?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. But these proceedings, especially those that involve murder, take a long time. For instance, in the examples we just reviewed, an event happened -- for instance, let us look at page -- just a moment. Let me take one of the recent examples, not to waste time. Page 9, the cases we just reviewed. If the time of commission is the 24th of April and the ruling to initiate proceedings was made on the 26th of May, that is a month after the crime was committed. In the other two cases the commission -- the perpetration was in May, and already in May the ruling to initiate proceedings was made. The interval between the perpetration and the decision to initiate proceedings is short, about a month. I should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the usual time, one month, approximately, it took to bring the ruling to initiate proceedings after completing all the preliminary actions such as detection, apprehension, investigation, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those specific conditions, it was really efficient work. Those are murders. But in the cases of theft and less grave crimes, the perpetrator would be apprehended on the same day in cases of crimes involving property. A good part of the crimes would already be under way before the courts, or even adjudicated, in the space of a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see from this paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, my question was whether these suspects or accused were convicted at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were. Some still have not received the judgement, I guess. This is the information that I can elicit from the general, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of these were convicted? I don't know if he knows that, but the description of the crime is clear. Some of these cases must have been referred to regular military courts after the termination of the state of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I have data ending with the 2001 as to how many were convicted. Some cases were decided, and some cases are still under way, ongoing. After 2001, I didn't monitor any longer. But for instance, if you look at murders, this is the type of case that would be complex and would take a longer time. But in those -- in simpler cases involving less serious crimes, I believe most of them have already been adjudicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you have your data with you now as of 2001?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell me that, please. Briefly. I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a similar review, a similar overview as to what cases were completed, what cases were referred to civilian courts, and in the final column you see the outcome of the proceedings for those cases that were finished. I have another survey yet concerning referrals to civilian courts, and the data I received from the latter. I can provide this to you to be translated and photocopied. You don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the sake of time, I would like the accused to proceed, and we'll deal with it after the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I, just before we do proceed, be clear about something, General. Can I take it that if there had been a judgement by 2001 in the cases we have been looking at, you would have reflected it in the document we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this paper, in this paper I'm holding right now, it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In tab --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the other document that has not been translated, there would certainly be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But the one that you're looking at as part of the examination by Mr. Milosevic, that's tab 18 of the bundle, can I take it that if there had -- if there had been a conviction by 2001, you would have noted it in this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now some of the cases have been referred to what is described as the district court, for example, the district court in Belgrade. That's a civilian court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. District and municipal courts are civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can I take it that you regarded it as appropriate to refer cases which might be described as war crimes to the civilian courts after the conflict was over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to clarify this immediately. Military courts do not have competence to go on processing a case after a person is demobilised, because most of these people were engaged from the reserve force. After the termination of the state of war, they ceased to be military personnel. If by that time an indictment has not been confirmed by the court, the case would be normally referred to the municipal or to the district court, depending on the gravity of the crime. Military courts would continue to process a case only if the person involved, the perpetrator or the accused, continues to be a military man. This concerns only the cases where a decision has been made by a military court. As for referrals, I have some additional data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, I don't know if you paid attention to -- to this last question by Judge Bonomy and what exactly he meant. He asked you if a judgement was made in all the cases indicated in this document.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all these cases were adjudicated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We won't go any more through this document, in keeping with your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, we have other cases dealing with voluntary and involuntary manslaughter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we move on, that's a completely different answer from the one you gave to me, General. My understanding -- and let's be clear we're looking at the same document. Have before you tab 18. Be absolutely sure the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And look at page -- look at page 6. My English version is page 6. It's headed, "Murder multiple." The first accused's name is Dragisa Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if by the year 2001 there had been a judgement in this case, would you have noted that in this document when you were compiling it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a column here where it says "referred to the district court in Pristina." That was done after an indictment was brought. So he was already indicted when his case was referred to the district court in Pristina, and then later on it was transferred to Nis. I have information that a hearing was scheduled -- the trial was scheduled, and I believe a judgement was brought here. I believe also -- I seem to remember that it was reversed on appeal, but I'm not sure about that. What it says here specifically is that the case was referred after an indictment was brought against this accused to the district court in Pristina, later moved to Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why did you not complete the column that says "Judgement"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the simple reason that I was no longer working on this subject matter. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's my question. You see, my question relates to the position as at 2001. Can you just concentrate on the question I'm asking you. Now, if there had been a result in that case by 2001, would you have reflected that result in this document when you were compiling it in 2001?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought that was the answer, and then Mr. Milosevic got a completely different answer from you, so I just wanted to be clear about the position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I answered the same. Maybe it was interpreted differently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I, too, understood him as giving the same answer, namely that all those cases in which judgements were made, judgements were brought, were reflected here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps just another clarification would be of assistance, if you allow me, please. We should look at the column dealing with grave robbery or felony theft. I don't know what page it is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a look at page 20 in the English version. That's grave incidents of robbery. There is noted down about the judgement, sentenced to three years and six months each. That judgement was entered into by the military court; is that right? So you noted down all the dispositions by the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy's question, as I understand it, is whether you noted down the judgement made by the civilian court referred to later if the judgement was made at the time of 2001 when you compiled this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had received a report, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That was precisely my question. You reflected those cases about which you received reports, which doesn't necessarily mean that you included all of them.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because in some cases I did not receive reports. There are both kinds in this overview. If I had received a report, then I would indicate what kind of judgement, if any, had been made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy also referred to this page about murders. Dragisa Petrovic is the first name, and there is something handwritten in the -- on this page.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In my copy, there is a handwritten note in the column Judgement, Nine years, seven years, nine years, and it's also added "war crime" down below. Is it only in my copy or do you have it in your copy as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the case of Dragisa Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I said a moment ago I followed that in the newspapers, and I indicated from my memory what the sentences were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it page 4 in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, page 4 in the Serbian version. I'll find it in just a moment. Here it is. In the English translation the Judgement column is empty. However, in the Serbian copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that, General, too?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I hope you do, Mr. Kwon, as well. It says nine years, then seven years, and then another term of seven years, and then at the end it says "war crime." That was not translated. It doesn't exist in the English version but it does in the Serbian photocopy, the judgements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We've found it. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to dwell on this table. I will skip over the voluntary and non-voluntary. And then we come to rapes. It is on page 16 of the English version; and for you, General, it is on page 14 of the Serbian text. Here we have a soldier who used force, together with some other soldiers, from a room in a house accommodating refugees. They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They forcibly removed an underaged person. All right. I don't want to read the names either, but judging by the names, I would say they were Albanian women, perhaps Roma women, I can't differentiate between the kinds of names. But Trivunovic, as printed, committed rapes, and the other person, Marinkovic, was unable to do so, et cetera, et cetera. But anyway, it's the 16th of April, crimes on the 16th of April, and then on the 24th of April -- rather, the time of crime was the 16th of April and ruling to initiate proceedings came on the 24th of April 1999 when an investigation was conducted. All the evidence was collected, all the necessary data, and legal proceedings were taken, and the general says that the indictment was raised as well, filed. Then once again out of a convoy of refugees so-and-so took aside an individual - I'm going to skip the name, but we can deduce on the basis of the name that it was an Albanian lady - took her to the sector where his union was -- unit was encamped. Another case of rape. The time of the crime was the 29th of May, the ruling to initiate proceedings came on the 24th of June, 1999. Then we have attempts at rape, attempted rape. And then several pages after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we move on to that, this is another page where the Serbian original at page 14 of the original has a handwritten passage that's not been translated. And if the Chamber thinks it would be helpful to get this sorted out as we go along, so does page 15 of the Serbian version, which I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. If the witness could help the Chamber. Could you read those handwritten parts on page 14.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Under number 1, in the judgement, we heard that a request was sent to the UNMIK courts at Kosovo for legal assistance to listen to the injured party, hear the injured party. So by the time that this report was compiled, the judgement came, I learnt that the court had asked for information and data and that UNMIK -- they asked UNMIK for assistance, legal assistance. They didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we have the 24th of April, 1999, as the time of crime.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the proceedings are still carrying on or were carried on in the district court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice also drew our attention to page 15. There was something written in hand there.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation here is the same as in the previous case. The proceedings are ongoing. They contacted the UNMIK courts in Kosovo, didn't receive any -- the assistance they required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to give any legal qualifications, but if we look at severe crimes of burglary with killings, these serious crimes, grave incidents of robbery and violence, to retain stolen goods, with murder involved. That's that page. And we see that the time of the crime was the 29th of March, 1999. It is page 19 of the English text, gentlemen. The ruling to initiate proceedings came on the 13th of April, that is to say two weeks later, and evidence was collected in that space of time, within a fortnight. And we're dealing here with seven perpetrators or accused, and they were all reserve soldiers, reservists. And it says that based on a prior mutual agreement they all went to the house of Uksin Uksini and this man fired at him with an automatic rifle and stabbed his wife Djevahira in the neck, killing both of them. They then took and kept gold jewellery, money and other valuables from the house. Then we come to B, brief description of crime. They took a vehicle, a car, and then I assumed killed the owner. And we come to C. Once again three individuals who killed or, rather, three people were killed during a burglary, which makes it seven accused in all, people accused of grave incidents of robbery and violence to retain stolen goods with murder. I assume that is how the qualification reads in the Criminal Code; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Might I be allowed to make an additional explanation at this point, please? We see here six individuals listed or, rather, they -- it says that six people were killed but are not shown in the summary representation of the crimes. So this should be recorded as well, where it says a summary report in the same tab when it comes to grave incidents of robbery. There is an empty column, and there we need to add these six persons killed. So that the number of victims in the victims column should be six more. In the summary review at the beginning of the tab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the statistics looked at the killings and represented them with a figure, whereas the robbery was accompanied with the killing of people. There was an omission there anyway. I should now like to ask you -- well, I don't want to deal with this further unless you have an additional statement to make, but I'd like to move on now to tab 17 on page 67 or, rather, chapter 17, page 67, and I'll try to find it in the English version. Chapter 17 starts on page 67. And as we can see from the contents, it gives a review of unknown persons who killed a number of individuals in Kosovo. So they are denoted as NN, persons unknown. The perpetrators are not known. The crimes are recorded. So that is on page 67. In Serbian. Page 67 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 75 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a summary review, as it says. Page 67 Serbian, 75 English. We know that thanks to Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It's page 75 of tab 18, not of tab 17.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, tab 18. That's how I understood it; we're dealing with tab 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain this table to us, please? It says "Person who committed crime," unknown. "Military prosecutor dismissed one charge, military prosecutor gathering intelligence from reports, court proceedings upon motion of the military prosecutor for conducting certain investigative measures, case deferred to competent public prosecutor." The total number is 598, number of persons killed. That's the summary report and that's the total number. I assume that this doesn't need any special explanation on your part, or would you like to give some?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about unknown persons, perpetrators of crimes, where the crime was uncovered but not the perpetrator, and the prosecutor takes certain steps in cases of that kind and so do the investigating organs. And in one case the prosecutor rejected the request because they were members of the KLA. And in the next column, with five cases, the military prosecutor collects information from the organs investigating the case and takes further steps. One case was referred to the court and the other to the public prosecutor. That is to say in cases where the prosecutor felt that the possible perpetrators of those crimes were not members of the army or were not military personnel and, therefore, those cases were referred to the competent district prosecutor. There were 11 such cases. We have a total figure of 598 persons, and three persons should be added there. They were left out by mistake, because three more persons were mentioned. So it is 395 -- 98 plus 3, which means 600-odd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify what you've just said. It was under number 2 on the following page. Now, did he reject the case because he learnt that there was no military unit in the region? Was that the reason or was there some other reason?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This criminal report was rejected because the military prosecutor found that they were not civilians but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to something else. On the next page, under number 2. What you've just explained to us, you said that the military judiciary did not prosecute because it wasn't under their competence to do so. Is that because he concluded that there was no military unit in the territory, in the area? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the district prosecutor is where the case was referred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to page 68 for a moment where we have the names and surnames and persons are listed as unknown, the time of perpetration is unknown, and then we have the place listed as Izbica where 144 fresh graves of unknown persons were uncovered. And the military prosecutor was informed thereof. The time when the proceedings were initiated was the 29th of May, 1999, which means that there was detection first, information gathered, and proceedings initiated on the 29th of May, 1999. And after that there's nothing else except current affairs.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to give an explanation? Exhumation was conducted, and the bodies were examined by a team, a forensic team from the Military Medical Academy, and they carried out a post-mortem on 101 bodies. They were able to identify a small number of those bodies but not the most part. And there were 144 fresh graves in all, and exhumation, investigations were conducted with 101 bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we passed the time to break. If it's a convenient time to break, we will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we were dealing with page 68 of the Serbian version. You have here, as we were saying, "Murders committed by persons unknown for which the military prosecutor is gathering intelligence from reports." That's the title. Will you please take a look at the table on that page. You started with number 1 and explain that to us, the Izbica place of crime, when the proceedings were initiated.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, it was on the 29th of May, 1999, when the case was uncovered. That is to say it was reported by the command of the unit who happened to be there during that period of time, and straight after that the prosecutor requested exhumation, which was conducted by a team of forensic experts from the Medical Military Academy in Belgrade, and they conducted the post-mortem and examination of 101 bodies. So during that same time, and that was sometime at the beginning of June, that is what happened. The prosecutor is still gathering information. But as the locality itself does not come under the legal jurisdiction of the federal state, Serbia and Montenegro as it is today, we have no access to the crime scene for us to investigate the case more fully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said the exhumation was performed by the competent authorities and that they -- it was a team of forensic experts from Medical Military Academy who conducted examinations.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The order was issued by the court in Kosovska Mitrovica for that to take place. It was not something that the military court of the Pristina Corps was able to, and then the investigating judge from Kosovska Mitrovica issued an order because without a court order you cannot Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exhumate bodies or conduct post-mortems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see that the time of the proceedings initiated was the 29th of May, 1999. Now, tell me about number 2. That relates to the municipality of Gnjilane, place of crime. There's no date as to when the proceedings were initiated.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a number of bodies were found in the area, it was not recorded for March to June 1999, 33 bodies in all, and the time the proceedings were initiated I have information that it was the 24th of May, 1999, and the SUP of Gnjilane informed the military prosecutor and the necessary steps were taken. So that was on the 24th of May, which means that this does go up to the 24th of May although that column and square is left empty, but according to when the military prosecutor was informed, that was on the 24th of May, 1999. And a request was made for gathering intelligence by the organs of investigation, and the case is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next you come to the place of crime which is Pirane, a village near Prizren. The bodies of five unidentified people were discovered, and we see that the proceedings were initiated on the 5th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. So this could have been before, and that's when the proceedings were initiated and a request made for intelligence to be gathered, the request coming from the military prosecutor. And it is the investigating organs that had to gather information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next case was 14 graves of unidentified people discovered in the Muslim cemetery in the village of Bijelo Polje. Time of crime, no date recorded there.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And this is interesting because it's not only when you come across the bodies of persons killed in the field but also when they come across graves which are not marked and freshly dug-out graves. So in those cases, too, the organs in question can suspect that a crime has taken place, and then they take all the necessary steps to investigate. In this case it was a Muslim cemetery. Probably they were members of the Muslim religion, Islam, so that could make it Albanians and others, because other people -- other Muslims live in Bijelo Polje too. So we can't see who reported the crime. Probably someone from the locality. But anyway, the authorities took the necessary steps in these cases, too, to determine the circumstances under which these persons were killed. And we're talking about May 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then under number 5 you have a case of 16 -- bodies of 16 unidentified people found in the village of Slovinje. The date the proceedings were initiated is the 16th of April, 1999, and it says "report submitted - deferred to district public prosecutor in Pristina." But that was later on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was deferred or referred on the 18th of January 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us anything more about that case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have here that an exhumation was conducted and the individuals identified, and -- so their identity was determined on the basis of exhumation, and then the case was deferred to the district public prosecutor in Pristina, as it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what Yugoslav law envisages in such situations when a crime was committed. This has to do with a number of killed persons who were found and when the perpetrator is unknown. What happens then when the suspect is unknown?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law is quite clear on that. Especially the prosecutor has a clear-cut task. There is a special file that the prosecutor opens for NN persons, persons unknown. The military prosecutor acts through military organs, and also it is the organs of the interior that have to take action. That is say, all law enforcement agencies, regardless of whether they are within the military or not, are supposed to work on such a case and to collect information because the perpetrator is unknown. Such a case remains open. The prosecutor keeps taking action, and therefore there is no statute of limitation that applies. At any rate, if this is a war crime, there is no statute of limitation. There can only be an absolute statute of limitation. So in the case of crimes when the death sentence is prescribed, then there is a period of 20 or even 40 years during which the prosecutor can institute proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, can I ask a question while we are with this document. It's the same document, murders committed by persons unknown. You said that in relation to category 5, you received the information that the victims were identified later. Have you received any similar information in relation to number 1, the victims -- 144 victims in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I did look at the exhumation documents, but I didn't really see all of them, and I did not find any identification. I only saw descriptions of all the ways in which this was done. But the doctor who carried out the post-mortem told me that there were some persons who were identified, but I did not receive any such information. So I do not have any accurate information about number 1, only what I heard, that some persons were identified. But I was not in a position to investigate that -- or, rather, not investigate. That's not the right word. I was not in the position to receive the right kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could you please now look at the investigations carried out in the case of perpetrators unknown. Just tell me whether this is clear enough or whether I understood it properly. This has to do with victims who had been identified. That is to say investigations had been completed and the victims had been identified, or is there some other difference also in view of the previous table? So number 1, 25 bodies were found, exhumed, and identified, namely, and then a list of names follows.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mid-April 1999, the village of Malo Ribare, Lipljan municipality. And the 24th of April, 1999, is the time when proceedings were initiated.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain investigative measures is the word used, and that means that it is the investigating judge who acts upon the request submitted by the prosecutor, and he takes certain measures, hence the wording. Also, you can see the court register number, "Ki," that is Krivicna Istraga, criminal investigation. "Kr" is a different situation. Prosecutor's register. So hence the two different words. So it is a question of whether the court or -- is going to take certain measures or whether it is going to be the law enforcement agencies, namely the police, that is going to take measures. The judge has the liberty to take measures that were not even required by the prosecutor. That's the difference involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to item 2. And you have said that the military judiciary did not institute criminal proceedings because they did not have jurisdiction. They considered themselves not to have jurisdiction because there was no military unit there.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of one person who was identified, it says that he was killed by a policeman.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was the Prokuplje district court that carried out the on-site investigation, and proceedings are taking place there in the case of two policemen. These proceedings are still under way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, you have number 3. The time is the 31st of May, 1999, and it says: "Following notification, nine bodies were found in the houses of Seljarin Grdjaliju."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a small typo. It is Grdjalija Seljarin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
