utterances.text: On the 31st of May, 1999, the investigating judge of the Pristina Corps military court went to the scene on the 5th of June 1999 and compiled a note on the incident. He found 13 7.62-millimetre cartridges. He learned that Florije Borsoti was the victim.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a woman. A few minutes ago -- and she witnessed the killing. We said a few moments ago that there were some other persons in an adjacent yard. So in addition to these nine bodies that were found in Grdjalija's yard, there were three other victims that were found in the neighbourhood, so total is 12. In tab 17 we have the report of the investigating judge. We see that there is a report and we see that he could not continue his investigation because fire was opened at him from the neighbouring houses. Hence he had to leave the crime scene, and he instructed the police to take appropriate measures in order to carry out an appropriate investigation once the situation is right for that. Even his vehicle had been hit by a bullet. This was a great difficulty for the investigation agencies. It was hard for them to get to the crime scenes because fire was opened at them although it was very obvious that they were going out to conduct an on-site investigation in police vehicles and the like. It was very obvious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just say a few more words about the next page, page 4, persons unknown, mid-April 1999. This is number 4. And it is the 7th of May, 1999, when investigating -- when proceedings were initiated. Could you please be so kind as to explain. You have a very detailed explanation here.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are a few points that are not quite clear. I managed to decipher it, if I can use that word. The military police organs informed the military court of the Pristina Corps investigating judge that there was a large number of bodies in the villages Dosevac. Dobrosevac is what is written here but that is a typo. It's Dosevac. Anyway, the date was the 7th of May, 1999, and the investigating judge was informed by the commander of the Glogovac police station that on the 3rd of May, 1999, he had been told on the 3rd of May, 1999, by Captain Rade Krsmanovic of the military post 1365 Raska that there were about 150 bodies in the village of Dosevac and 58 bodies in Gladno Selo. On the 23rd of April, 1999, the military police organs -- in the village of Gladno Selo. Before the police station commander had provided this information the military police organs had already been in the area and on the scene. The military police organs found a total of 20 bodies in the three yards, not as the preliminary information had said. Later on, further down, we see what they found. On the 30th of April, 1999, the bodies were found as described, by a VJ unit. Since member of the VJ did not commit these murders, the investigating judge did not order an exhumation. Colonel Orovic informed the investigating judge - that is the commander of a unit, Colonel Orovic - that -- I mean, whatever he says Dobrosevac it's supposed to be Dosevac. He says that the VJ units did not find any bodies in Dosevac or any traces that indicated that there had been any, but in the village of Dosevac, which is another village, he found about 140 bodies. VJ units were not stationed in the village before this. And he informs the investigating judge that it was impossible to carry out an on-site investigation there, and this is what the investigating judge says in his own report, which is included in the file, because units of the KLA entered the area with weapons and they did not allow any access. Colonel Pavlovic was head of the MUP team there, and they were given orders, and they were told to go to Gladno Selo and carry out an on-site investigation. So there is 140 bodies in Dobrosevac -- sorry, not Dobrosevac, Dosevac. Again I'm saying that there's a typo here. It's the village of Dosevac, the village of Srbica. And the total number of bodies is 160 in these two localities. And certain action was taken, of course. The investigating organs cannot act if there is fighting in the area. Then they are not in a position to carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I don't think there is any need to go into further detail in this regard. Tell me, General, what was the situation in view of all these proceedings that were initiated, that is to say investigations carried out, information collected, et cetera? What was the situation at the beginning of October 2000, namely at the time when I and some other persons who are included in this Kosovo indictment ceased to hold office?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these cases were discovered during the state of war, all of them. All were dealt with in a certain form and to a certain level as much as possible. Apart from that, there is no information stating that anything new was discovered, any new incident regarding which action could be taken in this form. So this is the situation as it was when the state of war ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. While the state of war was still in force, to the best of your knowledge, because you toured courts of law and other agencies, what about our law enforcement agencies? Were they in a position to discover all violations of humanitarian law that were carried out in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that there was a war going on and that there was fighting in this relatively small area and where there was a great concentration of armed personnel, it was not possible to discover all the perpetrators or to see all the crimes that had been committed. It would be an illusion to expect to be able to do that within such a short period of time. It would also be an illusion to believe that a perpetrator would speak up and say that he had committed a crime. There must have been many of them who have a mutual solidarity, and they know that what they did is punishable by very severe sentences. Not all officers were in a position to do something, especially in view of the dispersion of units involved. Units could not concentrate because they were targeted by NATO Air Force. The alax [as interpreted] would discover them if they would be in concentrations of more than ten persons. That's why they had to be dispersed, and the situation was such that therefore, objectively speaking, the military officers in the area could not establish complete control over their subordinates, especially not the law enforcement organs that are at the level of the bigger units. They went to where corpses were found. They also went to graveyards where they found freshly dug graves. They went wherever it was possible to find the traces of a crime that had been recently committed. They went wherever they were aware of something like that, but they could not go to places that they did not know about. Also, when our forces withdrew, jurisdiction ceased to exist as far as our agencies were concerned. If this had remained within our jurisdiction, it is certain that there would have been visible results far exceeding those that were achieved so far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to put a very clear question to you. Do you know of any single crime that constitutes a violation of international humanitarian law that Yugoslav organs found out about and did not initiate appropriate proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such case because that would have been sheer nonsense as far as the judiciary is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, bearing in mind all your previous answers as well as the fact that you were a lawyer, a judge, a prosecutor, did you have an opportunity of familiarising yourself with the content of the Kosovo indictment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you compare the allegations contained in the indictment with the information that our military judiciary had?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did make some comparisons and some comparative reviews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several localities --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just where are we going? Is the witness going to give us an opinion on that very series of decisions that it's for this Trial Chamber to make? Is that what the accused wants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can decide after we hear some comparison he's going to say. I will consult. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you reformulate your question in a more specific way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Certainly, Mr. Kwon, I will phrase it very specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, General, since you compared the two, tell me, to what degree is there a certain coincidence between what was established by our competent authority - when I say "competent" I mean the courts and all the other judiciary, including all the cases that were reviewed in our country - and allegations in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take the case of Racak, which is not under review here, we have an 80 to 90 degree coincidence in the case of Izbica village, because there were 144 fresh graves, 101 bodies were autopsied, but we have to bear in mind that the indictment was revised several times - three times, more exactly - and in the summary review that we saw before, the total number is 120. So it is almost complete coincidence between the two. There are another two localities where the information coincides. For instance, the indictment mentions Sudimlje and Gornje Sudimlje whereas in our information we have Donje Sudimlje. Those are places in the same area, same municipality, and there is also a coincidence between the two documents in Grdjalija where our investigative organs were not able to finish their work because of the circumstances, but the information coincides in cases involving death. As for robberies and other crimes since -- crimes against property, since it involves a broad spectre of crimes. In cases of aggravated robbery, for instance, we have clear descriptions of what exactly was taken without inventories, but the property in question was found in the possession of perpetrators. Large numbers of peanuts, et cetera, 200 kilos, et cetera, something that the perpetrator must have stolen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, I couldn't follow when you mentioned Racak and Izbica village. Did you mean that Racak is in Izbica village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Racak is a completely separate incident of the 15th of January where the competent judiciary organs of the civilian courts in Pristina processed. That was not taken into account in the indictment -- in the summary review, sorry, but it is mentioned in the indictment. I am setting that case aside. Izbica is a completely separate locality where the number of victims is approximately the same. However, the locality is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I follow. There should be a period between the sentences. Yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it the case that the military -- that in the case of Izbica, military judiciary organs had specific information whether the victims were civilians or KLA members.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Extraordinarily leading observation for which there is absolutely no material foundation, unless I've missed it. I'm particularly interested to know what this witness is going to provide by way of his foundation material in relation to Izbica, and so that last question rather spoils the purpose of examination and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reformulate your question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking a perfectly neutral question. I asked about a case that the general has mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- were, rather, the military judiciary in a position to establish in all these various cases whether the victims were civilians or KLA members?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of only one case where it was established that victims were members of the KLA, and the military prosecutor dismissed the criminal report. In all the other cases, it was not possible to establish from the initially available evidence whether any of the victims were civilians or KLA members, except, of course, in the cases where the victims were women and children, because in most of the cases it was not possible to identify or decide whether somebody was a civilian or not, only on the basis of whether they wore a uniform or not. A uniform is no indicator, just as the -- just as civilian clothing is not enough to establish that somebody was not a member of armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, why was it that the judiciary did not complete its investigation in the case of Izbica, for instance?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the very simple reason that the military prosecutors withdrew from Kosovo on the date envisaged by the -- by the Military Technical Agreement. It was only up to that date that they could work. And they could only gather evidence up to that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those cases where investigations were carried out to establish the circumstances and identify perpetrators, were there such cases that were not covered by the indictment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. All the cases that you can find in my documentation, in this summary review. In all those localities, appropriate investigations were carried out whenever it was objectively possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, according to the data that is available to you, based on those investigations and investigative measures carried out, and they were carried out in all the localities, what numbers are involved, and what is the correlation between that number and the numbers cited in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for cases where the perpetrator is unidentified, there is a total of 601. This is incomplete data. So 601 unidentified perpetrators. And as for known perpetrators, we have 42 or 43 victims. So the total is 645 victims involved in both types of cases. That is a precise number. In the indictment, the last revised, amended indictment, the number is 608. So it's approximately the same or very similar. As for description of crimes, it is vague in the indictment. It says "around," "approximately," et cetera. So in the last amended indictment the number is 701. In the previous second amended indictment the number was lower, around 400 for the indictment of the 22nd of May. These are approximate numbers, although every death, every victim is important. But if you ask me about correlation, there is a relatively high degree of coincidence. Our investigative organs detected, uncovered a great number of crimes and perpetrators, and now that this Tribunal has access to the documentation and our investigative organs no longer have access to the area, that is the number we have to work with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is all this information public?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, relatively speaking, because investigative organs do not make their information public to prevent panic while investigation is going on, but anybody who is interested can gain access to this data, because all the -- all the actions, all the proceedings are public. They're not closed to the public by any means. It's just that the information is not published, publicly announced, but it is accessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your entire experience, General, from the period we are discussing now, what according to your knowledge was the principal position of the highest military and civilian authorities regarding crimes and their perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from all these actions that were taken at the level of the Supreme Command Staff and the judiciary bodies in keeping with the legislation, and if we look at the measures accompanied by the enforcement of those laws -- that accompanied the enforcement of those laws, we cannot see that there was no action, no measures taken that disregarded the requirement to comply with international humanitarian law. All the measures were taken to prosecute perpetrators in every case where a violation of international humanitarian law was uncovered in the entire territory, including Kosovo and Metohija. We can see this from our surveys and overviews. As for the police, the military prosecutors, the military courts and everybody who was in charge of reporting crimes, everybody made a maximum effort. No case was neglected or forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I asked you specifically: What according to your knowledge was the principal position of the highest authorities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To prevent crimes, of course. And if crimes take place, that they should be prosecuted and punished. This is the fundamental guideline, the fundamental principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge based on all the information you received from all organs, everybody you came in contact with, was there ever an idea in circulation that they should be killed and persecuted in order to expel them from the territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. There can be no question of that. Not even clandestinely could there have been such an idea, because our competent authorities did everything to prevent any murder. It would be an illusion to believe that for a moment. If we compare the number of victims which is currently recorded as a thousand to 1.200, although it's very difficult to operate with approximate numbers, that is -- that would be impossible with such a large number of police in the military in Kosovo at the time. If you just allow me. In the area of Djakovica, there is reference here to some refugees who were moving out because of the fighting between Yugoslav armed forces and the KLA. It was considered a liberation army of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just another question. There is a paragraph in the indictment dealing with the highest political and military leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters beg the accused to repeat the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you repeat the question, or could you repeat the paragraph from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 19, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it says: "... while holding positions of superior authority, Slobodan Milosevic and the others are also individually criminally responsible for the acts or omissions of their subordinates, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. A superior is responsible for the acts of his subordinates if he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit such acts or had done so, and the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish their perpetrators." So from all you know, from all you were able to follow and document, is there any coincidence between this allegation that he is responsible if he is responsible, if he knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit such acts or had done so and the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't hold water, because all the competent authorities, all the professional services established at the level of the Supreme Command Staff were tasked, were legally bound and received orders to do their utmost to prevent crimes, and if crimes were detected, to find and punish the perpetrator. So if you want to find a cause and effect connection between omissions or failures of our organs, there is no such connection. That is something basic in criminal law. I know that from my own work, because I had direct access to all the information about what is being done on the -- on the ground. The chain of responsibility does not -- is uninterrupted there. You cannot establish responsibility in this case. If you speak about reasonable measures, all the reasonable measures were taken in view of the time and the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an experienced soldier and lawyer, can you tell me, was there a measure that could have been taken and was not taken?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, because some measures were impossible to take. You cannot have a policeman and a prosecutor following every soldier on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are coming close to the end of this examination. But apart from the question of Kosovo, I just have a few more short questions for you in view of your own activities in the military judiciary, and I will be able to complete my examination in chief within one or two minutes to get through it all. But let's go back to the beginning of the 1990s. What was your role in the case with respect to the well-known killing of the soldier from a firearm and an attempt at killing another soldier by strangling him in Split at the beginning of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. That was on the 6th of May, 1991. It was in front of the headquarters of the military naval district where some large-scale demonstrations were held with the aim of provoking the command, and this particular case I was the prosecutor in the case. It went to the Split military -- from the Split military court and referred to the military court in Sarajevo in order to create the necessary conditions for unimpeded legal proceedings, and I was the prosecutor in that case. It was about the killing of a soldier. His name was Bjesovski. Bjesovski was the name of the soldier. He was a Macedonian soldier. Another one, Svetlance, and the driver of that combat vehicle was also a Macedonian. He was -- they were all members of the duty guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you what your role was, and you said you represented the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in any other case with respect to the Vukovar case in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before moving on, was there an accused person in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who was the -- in the case you've just referred to, the one involving the Macedonian soldier, the case --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. There were four accused; Ivan Begonja. He's the one that tried to strangle the soldier. Then there was Zvonaric, another -- four of them, four accused, and they were civilians from Split, the town of Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did the military prosecutor have jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the attack was an attack on military personnel in the course of doing their duty. They were on guard duty for the command, and therefore it came under the military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that -- does that mean that in Kosovo the military prosecutor investigated attacks on Yugoslav army soldiers by Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you don't have the particulars of that with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have the particulars of that, no. But the total number of persons killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'll just follow on from what Mr. Bonomy said, and I'd like to draw your attention to tab 19 now, General. Tab 19 is a review of the losses in the Yugoslav army, officers, non-commissioned officers, soldiers, contractual soldiers, reserve officers, reserve soldiers, and so on and so forth. And it says the causes of death during the aggression in combat operations, 546 persons; from NATO planes 248 or 45.4 per cent, under the effects of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we could pause there. We have a note that it hasn't been translated. Could you -- could the B/C/S version be put on the ELMO so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Since it is a table, you're able to follow the figures quite easily, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it says in the note at the bottom, and I hope it's on the ELMO now, the note at the bottom of the page says the cause of death during the aggression in combat operations, and then in brackets 546 persons; under the effects of NATO aviation, 248 persons or 45.4 per cent people were killed. The victims of Siptar terrorist forces, the number there is 246 individuals or 45.1 per cent; from the effects of mines, once again the KLA, 33 persons lost their lives, or 6.0 per cent; and other reasons, miscellaneous, brackets, NATO and the Siptar terrorist forces later identified as having been killed, 19 of those or 3.5 per cent. So Mr. Bonomy asked you whether you were -- had the authority of establishing these deaths, and here we can see -- or, rather, take a look at the total number now, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the losses during NATO aggression in the combat operations during the armed conflicts. I understood the question to be that he was asking about crimes which were outside combat operations because it was linked to the events in Split where there were no armed conflicts at that moment. So that was the answer I gave along those lines. I said I didn't have information of that kind. But there were cases of that kind in Kosovo and Metohija where, in peacetime, crimes were committed against soldiers. And these cases were dealt with by the military court in Nis, but I didn't present that kind of information and data here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, these are serious losses, large numbers, several hundred people killed in the operations. I quoted the causes a moment ago. I don't want to repeat it. But is it possible that they could have been killed by unarmed civilians, because quite obviously they were -- or is it quite obviously the case that people died or were killed in struggles over a very violent enemy?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all -- this is all information from combat reports where the commanders of each unit ascertained and established the deaths resulting from terrorist armed formations of Albanians in Kosovo and these are differentiated from the NATO aviation victims. So these are the losses of the Yugoslav army members and not the losses of the MUP. We have a column of people killed before the aggression. Forty-five soldiers and officers died before the aggression from the effects of KLA armed formations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I omitted to tender these remaining tabs that we dealt with in detail into evidence. I think the last one was tab 15 that was admitted into evidence, and I'd like to tender 16, 17, 18 and 19, the remaining tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit them. However, those parts which contain the names of the rape victims will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this in closing, two short questions linked to your professional service. Did you take part in any court cases linked to the Vukovar cases in the autumn of 1991, Vukovar and its environs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to that event, I acted as the investigating judge although I was present at the military court in Belgrade but this was pursuant to a request for the military prosecutor to take steps linked to the event that happened in Vukovar, in Ovcara, and I spent -- I undertook certain investigative steps and then the documents were sent to the prosecutor who then referred the case to the district prosecutor in Belgrade because he found that he -- this did not come under his authority and competence to try the perpetrators. And also I was the presiding officer of a court chamber which at the request of this Tribunal asked that the three persons be taken into custody. The request was refused because there was domestic criminal law on the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which did not provide for the possibility of extraditing nationals, Yugoslav nationals to a foreign country and foreign institution. Those provisions have now been amended in the constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, that completes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that independence of the judiciary is important in your system. Are you a fully independent person coming to give evidence here yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No connections with any vested interest or political interests that underlie the cases we're dealing with?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No particular loyalty to this accused?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None except my professional approach to the matter in hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of interest, when did you last visit Russia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I've been abroad, outside the boundaries of the SFRY. I've never been to Russia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at tabs 17 and 18 initially, because I want you to tell us this: Can we find in either tab 17 or 18 any recorded conviction of an individual for a war crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tab 17, it is the report by the military court in Nis, they took it in chronological order, and in the columns we see the judgements, where the judgement was made. And in tab 18, I'd like to draw attention to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tab 17 because I'm afraid I've only had a translated version of this document for a day, and I had lots of other things to do. We've had a version of the B/C/S document for about a week. In tab 17, is there anything there that constitutes a war crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just point us to one so that we can all understand what is a war crime and how it was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is. In tab 18 you can see that. Just so that I can connect the two. If you find the page in tab 17. Find page 43 in tab 17. Under number 7. I don't know what the page is in English. 43, number 7. Then you'll find the individuals listed. War crimes, Article 142 of the Criminal Code linked to Article 22. So you have that on page 43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us a second. We've got to page 43 in the B/C/S, and we're going to find it in the English if we can. This is the page -- this is the page --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's Slobodan Stosic. The page heads with --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the others too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ivan Nikolic, and we'll just see if we can find that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Stosic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just wait a minute. There's no point in our following it or trying to follow it unless we can find the English, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the report number? There are several reports. Tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In tab 17, it's number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Trial page 56, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Yes, absolutely right. We're now on the same -- on different page but effectively the same pages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you want to tell us little bit about Slobodan Stosic, and you say this is recorded as a war crime. Just explain further, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 7 and number 10, another war crime. And the prosecutor here qualified the crime as such wherever there was an order from a superior officer that a crime was committed if the perpetrators committed the crime. So here we have the suggestions that the crime be committed and they perpetrated the crime. And this is a classical example. He cannot bypass the superior officer. Wherever there was a superior officer ordering somebody to do something and the subordinate soldier committed the crime, that was considered a war crime. Where there was no superior officer having ordered or kept quiet about, turned a bind eye to, et cetera, then it wasn't considered a crime of that nature. So you have this case in point, the one you were interested in, number 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am interested in it, and I just want to see how we see that it's reported as a war crime. What's different about it than anything else. Is it that it's under Article 142 that shows its a war came?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Article 142 is a crime, a war crime against the civilian population pursuant to the Criminal Code of Serbia and Montenegro. At the time it was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the facts of the Slobodan Stosic case is probably well known to you because this was a man who took some prisoners out of the gaol, didn't he, and he took them down to Kosovo and -- did he take them down to Kosovo to kill people? What was the nature of the crime? Was that what he did?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is. I'll read it out. So the people who were there, he ordered them, the subordinates --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can we find what you're reading from?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A description of the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you see --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In tab 18 you'll find a description of the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You're now in tab 18, and what page in tab 18?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes. It is page 2 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was the only one in tab 17 and thus far the only one in tab 18 that's a war crime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's one other one on the following page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But before we move on from Stosic, who complained about Stosic's crime?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the table here we see Article 142, which relates to all of them, not -- it's 142. Several Articles 142 are referred to. Wherever it says Article 142, I assume, and I assume General Gojovic knows this, in the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia is a war crime. Article 142 is a war crime. Was that clear from his answer? So it's not only -- doesn't only apply to Stosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Who complained about Stosic's and Palinkos' and Mijatovic's and Miskovic's behaviour?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was uncovered in mid-April, and a report was sent to the prosecutor and the prosecutor undertook proceedings. I don't know who informed the prosecutor about the event. I don't have that here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, somewhere the underlying papers will exist that show how it was that this war crime charge was initiated, but you can't help us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's in the documents of the criminal case, and I didn't have access to the papers because it was sent to the district court in Kraljevo. I wasn't an investigator and therefore didn't look at the documents. But everything is recorded there, who took what steps and when in the files, the binder for that particular case, whereas these are brief entries about what the case -- of what the case was about, a brief description of the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The case against these men, has it been discontinued?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what result?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trial continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what result?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pretty serious case, isn't it? Throwing people into a well and setting light to the bodies? Throwing bodies into a well and setting light to them. Pretty serious case. You can't help as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a serious case, yes, but as soon as it was referred to the district court, it was no longer under my sphere of competence. I did ask -- I did ask to see the papers, and the first instance judgement was revoked, but I didn't record this because I learnt about the case later on. So when I drew up this column --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go to number 10. This is the next in tab 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me be a bit clear on this matter. Could page 56 of tab 17 be put on the ELMO. General Gojovic, in item number 7 you see Mr. Stosic here, and at the second last column it says proceedings against Mr. Stosic discontinued. So that's why he does not appear in page 4 of tab 18, and he is the highest -- he has the highest rank amongst them. He was the lieutenant colonel while the others were reserve privates. Do you happen to remember why proceedings against this Slobodan Stosic discontinued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the information I received from the prosecutor orally, it was ascertained that he didn't order them to do that but when they were uncovered, in order to justify their acts, they said that they had received orders and that's why the case came -- the proceedings were launched against Stosic. But once this was ascertained, the proceedings were discontinued and continued against the other individuals. But we can see the records of this in the military court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we move on from that, there being some potential ambiguity in the way things are recorded, the five reserve privates -- the three reserve privates, the one private and the perpetrator unknown, at least in this record, had they themselves, the perpetrators, been in prison and taken out from prison for the purposes of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such information that they were there previously. I don't know about that. I don't know where you get this information that they were in prison beforehand. They could have been sent to prison only because they committed this crime.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I cannot find it, the English translation now in this big bundle, but in the Serbian language it's quite clear what it says, and this is probably what confused Mr. Nice and that's why he put the question. In Serbian it says since they were taken out of detention - I mean this is in reference to the victims - they were brought to the wall of a house and fire was opened at them. These soldiers took people out of detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice is well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the accused's intervention. I may come back to this topic next week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now go to number 10 on tab 17, which is the only other one I think you're going to tell us referred to as an Article 142 matter, therefore a war crime.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Despite being a war crime, it was simply handed over to the district court in Valjevo, and do we know anything about what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that this case was deferred during the investigation because this was a reserve officer. He was demobilised, and then it was the district court in Valjevo that the case was deferred to, and I just knew that the investigation was under way. I did not have any other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that takes care of tab 17. But before we pass from tab 17, it's worth observing, isn't it, that a great number of cases were convicted for matters like stealing cars, sets of tools, money, things like that, with prison sentences recorded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there appear to have been the resources available in the judicial systems to bring to conclusion comparatively trivial cases in the time with which we're concerned. Comparatively trivial. I'm not suggesting that stealing someone's car is not of gravity to the person.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to tab --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just explain. It's because these are simple cases where it's easy to rule and the evidence is quite clear. But in case of complex proceedings, it requires a great deal of expertise and forensic expertise. If a particular object is stolen, it is easy to see the evidence, and it's easy for the courts to deal with that, and no expertise is required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. And before we move to tab 18 and since you raise it, to investigate the more serious crimes also requires access to sources of information, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you as the military judicial system presumably had ready access to relevant sources of information if you wanted them; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that we had. The sources of information that we did not have access to, we did not. It is on site that one acquires first information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You as the military investigator -- just assume for the time being that on a particular day at a particular time a VJ tank or tanks was or were seen to be deployed. Two things: First, in a well-regulated army, the location and deployment of tanks would be recorded, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the conditions in which the tank is deployed. You see, this is not front-line fighting. The area where this was taking place is rugged terrain, so patterns cannot be applied of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- let me tie you down a little bit more. If a tank was deployed on a particular date in a town, it doesn't matter what town, near to Pristina, it would be possible to work out from which unit that tank came, and you as the military judiciary and prosecutors one way or another would be able to get access to the records showing what the tank commanders were doing on the given day, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is some possibility on the condition that this commander knows at every moment where his tank is. A tank would not be in the same place for the entire day. Such a tank would not survive or, rather, its a crew would not survive until nightfall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your general answer. What I want you to help me with is this: There's a lot of evidence that tanks were deployed around Racak on the day that it was attacked and that they were firing into Racak in a way that people have said is criminal because it was inevitably disproportionate. I'd like you to tell us, please, what steps the Serbian-Montenegrin military judiciary took to investigate the tanks that attacked Racak.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no tank attack against Racak. I don't know where you get this information that you refer to just now. Secondly, it was the district court in Pristina that was in charge of the proceedings regarding Racak. Units were deployed in their positions far away from Racak. It is only after the fighting that they took some kind of combat order for the sake of their own protection. If somebody opened fire, it was mostly out of fear, probably, but the army did not take part in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all it was the district court in Pristina who was responsible so your unit wouldn't be. Then the second answer is that the units were deployed in positions far away from Racak but I don't know what your source of information for that. Your third answer is that it's only after the fighting that they took some kind of combat. Are you giving answers or are you trying to protect a position, General Gojovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not say that the units, after fighting, took part in combat. I do not have information that the units of the army of Yugoslavia took part in an armed conflict in Racak. I do not have such information. They were in the broader area. I cannot say that they were not in the broader area. I had the opportunity of talking to one officer, that is to say the commander who was there in -- at his command post, was it Djakovica or Glogovac, and he came to the position only subsequently, to the position where his unit was. So what happened in Racak has no influence over all of this. I mean, except for the fact that the units were in the broader area. But they did not take part in this. I do not have the kind of information that you have and no such information was available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that might be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before I turn from Racak, I overlooked at your very first answer about Racak, was that the event hadn't happened at all. How if you conducted no investigation were you able to offer that opinion to the Chamber that the attack by the VJ didn't happen at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. At that time on the 15th of January I was president of the military court in Belgrade, so it was not under the jurisdiction of that court. I have this unofficial information that the units of the army of Yugoslavia did not take part in this. I did not have occasion to act in any official capacity with regard to that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, you're a judge, or you've been a judge, and is the position you're now a lawyer? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Now I'm a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you've been a lawyer, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know how important it is to leave for judges the determination of factual issues on the basis of evidence and yet your immediate response to my question to you about Racak was there was no tank attack against Racak. Is that a sentence you'd now like to withdraw, bearing in mind it's the Judges who have to deal with the facts of this case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that it is the Judges who decide about that. It's not that I decide whether a statement will be considered in this way or that way. I just said that as far as I know, the members of the army of Yugoslavia did not attack Racak, did not take part in any such thing, as far as I know. I said that as a private individual, not in any official capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Do we have to distinguish in your evidence, then, and perhaps you would be helpful enough to tell us when we do, between answers you give in an official capacity and answers that you give as a private individual? Is that what we're going to have to do as we assess you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I said something as a private individual. Until now, I did not say anything like that. I just said, when asked about my knowledge, that I learned of these things in passing. I was never in a position to act in an official capacity in dealing with that. This is the only statement I've made here as a private individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I turn from tab 17, can I draw to the Court's attention that immediately after page 13 in the B/C/S version and immediately before page 14 there are some documents in Cyrillic that I wish to ask questions about but they haven't yet been translated. For some reason, they've been omitted. I understand from Ms. Anoya that the matter is being investigated and we will come back to it next Tuesday. I imagine the Court's papers will be similarly composed to mine, but it's between pages 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shall we turn, then, General, to tab 18. I'm still with the question of the issue of what's shown and revealed war crimes. So if we go in the English page 4, we've already looked at that, just to start our journey through the document. Go to page 2 in your version, page 4 in ours, we see the one we've already looked at and we know what happened there. Then we go to number 6 on page 5 in the English and page 3 in the Serbian. Stevan Jekic. Do we know anything about what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that a few moments ago. This case was referred, in the investigation stage, to the Valjevo district court and they continued the investigation. I'm not aware of the outcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was convicted or acquitted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More important, can you help me, please, with how it was that this matter was brought to the attention of authorities so that they investigated it to the degree that they did?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a brief description here about what this was all about, who reported about this, and then the investigation started and he was no longer a military person at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stop. I want to know who reported it. Do you follow me? Simple question. Because I want to know why, according to this table, some action was taken. Now, can you help me, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody reported it. I do not have information who it was who reported it. However, in the record, in the file of the case, there is such information, but I did not have the file in my hands. I did not have insight into it. This is information from the register where there is just brief contents of the cases that are being dealt with. But the files are with the court --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and a request can be made to obtain them. I'm sorry -- I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Gojovic, we're going to come to what happens to requests made to you and your government for material of this kind in due course, trust me, but I want to know now, is the register the underlying material that you relied on for all these cases that you tabulated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The register and the report of the military court. That is reliable information. And also when I required additional information, I would ask verbally the prosecutor or the president of the court to check some information out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And bearing in mind the answers you gave to the accused this morning, can you at the moment remember any other examples where you had to ask for supplementary information before either composing this table of investigations or where you had to seek additional information from an investigator in order to be able to give the answers to this Court today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not prepare myself especially for this here. I sought the information earlier. I sought this information from the courts to which the cases were referred. From some I did receive information, from others I didn't. From those I did, I used this information for compiling these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this additional information can be seen. If you wish, I can write about it more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go to the next table. We looked at this entry, page 6 of the English and page 4 of the Serbian, already, because this is the one that had a little bit of additional writing about the sentences of seven, nine, and seven years that were imposed. We will come back to the rest of the writing in due course because there are a couple of words and we'll have to see what you can tell us about those, but just tell us as to this one, numbers 1, 2 and 3 on English page 6, on Serbian page 4, what was your source of information? What was the source of information that led to this inquiry? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every column, it says whether the report was submitted or not, whether such information was known or not. There is no entry here, and this was done on the basis of the register, and that is not recorded in the register who this information was obtained from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can't help us, the answer no will do. There was dealt with under Article 47, as we see at the head of the page, so it wasn't dealt with as a war crime. However, this is the only occasion it may be when the words "war crime" appear, because they appear in the handwritten annotation on page 4 of the Serbian, underneath the recording of the number of years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have this information, but I do know that the prosecutor changed the charges, and it is certain that the charges were changed during the proceedings. But I did not follow the trial later. During the trial, the prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be my mistake entirely, and I do apologise if it is, but I hope my questions are comparatively straightforward. There appears on page 4 the handwritten notation recording a finding of war crime; correct? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you got this note. I do not have this note in this survey of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The handwritten -- page 4 of the Serbian, the handwritten entry, nine years, seven years, and seven years, and then there are two words underneath it. What do you say those words say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I notice the general is looking at the ELMO. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two words underneath the sentences of seven years. What are those words?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "War crime."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who wrote those words?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote those words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your table, General. You produced, you've prepared it, and you've brought it to court. Who wrote those words?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, lest there be any misunderstanding, I have brought my surveys. I have them here. But this is not my handwriting. This is not my handwriting. This is an entry that somebody made subsequently. I don't have any such thing on my documents. It's somebody -- yes. Well, never mind. But I know unofficially and from the newspapers that the charges were changed in this case, that it was -- that he was charged with a war crime, and that the first instance judgement was revoked and that the trial has been reinstituted. So I don't know if this is some -- I mean, I don't know about this myself. I don't have firsthand knowledge, but I have read in the newspapers that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this reflect, then, that the policy of the military courts was to charge matters as crimes other than war crimes but that on this particular occasion another lawyer getting seized of the matter gave it its correct title?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain it to me any other way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Go on, then.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain. The military prosecutor was committed to go with the highest, the most severe charge. If he does that, he always has the possibility to change the charge to a less severe one. However, if he starts with a less serious charge, he cannot commute it to a more serious one even if it turns out that the crime in question is a more serious one. That is why this was done that way. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll move on because -- in order to save time. This is the position, isn't it: There's no other crime in your tab 18 that is identified as a war crime at all. They're all categorised as domestic crimes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ending with this last number, you have this information, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I found out later that another four persons were charged with war crimes. We have that in the survey, the summary overview. A total of four persons were charged with war crimes, as we see from the overview, at the time. Another four were charged with war crimes later. They are not covered by this table. And a more serious crime was commuted or, rather, more serious charges were commuted to less serious charges on the decision of the district prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so good as to return, then, to page 68 of the Serb version and page 76 of the English which we can lay on the overhead projector. Again, just to -- I underline the point that I've been getting you to confirm, this page of the table is headed Article 47. It's not a war crime, despite the fact that 144 fresh graves of unidentified persons were found at Izbica and, as your table asserts, proceedings were initiated on the 29th of May, 1999, well before the conflict ended and while your courts were still in operation. So the general question is, please, why on earth wasn't this incident manifestly likely to be a war crime investigated as a war crime if you were doing your jobs properly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you don't seem to want to accept the explanation that the prosecutor had in mind. The prosecutor is the one who decides which charges to press, and he decides on this one because it entails the death sentence or the minimum prison sentence of ten years. If he qualifies it as a war crime, the minimum sentence is five years, and that why the prosecutor seems to have made this decision. It is easy to amend the indictment and commute the charges and requalify it as a war crime. War crime sounds better for the press, but under our national legislation, this particular charge entails a much harsher sentence than a war crime. That's why the prosecutor decided on these charges, because he's able later to change it if he wants to. You want to say that the prosecutor should have qualified this as a war crime from the start to satisfy justice. That would have had the contrary effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hadn't put it in those terms, General Gojovic, but in a sense you're quite right. But let's move on. Yes, I would suggest that to you; categorising war crimes in another way is a way of hiding collectively from the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look just for the last time at this page, although I'll have to return to it next week, because what you told us about the other place that may be covered in our indictment was something I haven't yet been able to prepare, but let's look at Izbica. I haven't been able to prepare, not knowing you were going to say at all. Izbica, initiated on the 29th of May, 1999, according to this table, and I ask you as I have with all the other -- I'm sorry. First of all, apart from the other village to which you've referred, this is the only matter in the Kosovo indictment covered in your table, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there are another two that could have qualified, but this is the only one that actually appears in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want your help, please, with why it was that this one got pursued and, as we can see on the basis of your table, comparatively early. Why was it that it got pursued?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Compared to this case, this location with fresh graves were found, the unit commander -- the commander of the unit which arrived there at the time reported that there are fresh graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Remember you told me not so very many minutes ago that your source of information for preparation of this table was - I can't remember what the name of the document is, but was another document - a register. Do you remember that you told me that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Remember I asked you questions about when you needed to go to seek further information in order to give evidence to this Court? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the face of page 76 or whatever it is. I'm sorry, I've lost it again now -- 68, I think. When we look at that, unless I've missed it, and you must help me with this, there is absolutely no reference to a unit finding an unmarked grave, let alone to a commander of a unit, is there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this original register, this piece of information does appear. It was a unit from Krusevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got it there so I can have a look at it? Because it doesn't appear on the document that we've got here.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll look for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though I'm pressed for time, I'm going to give you, with the Court's leave, enough time to --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. We can look at it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to see it today, if I can.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's somewhere in this material. I can't find it right now. I can't even open up all these pages to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and review over the days between now and when this court will sit again on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has been copied here in your services, and this material can be found under tab 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You're looking at tab 17. In which case it may be there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That piece of information is there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just see if we can find it, because if it's there we can move on, to a degree.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. Here under this tab. Under item 3 in tab 17. Fresh graves, 144 graves in village Izbica discovered by unit --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's under tab 17, at the end. There is an annex, a text there, report by the military prosecutor. The last report by the military prosecutor in that tab. The heading is "To the supreme military prosecutor in Belgrade from the military prosecutor in Nis."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the page number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end, there is no page number. It's prosecutor's report annexed to this tab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think we've seen this before. I'll just check, if I may. And it's not one of the untranslated --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be in your binder as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes photocopying errors occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The short answer, Your Honour, is it hadn't been included. Would Your Honour just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are a number of documents here that haven't been translated, and I see the documents that I have identified as not having been translated I think are included in the middle of this document. It may be that the better course would be for this document to be photocopied in full and provided to the parties today if that's something that the Chamber could organise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Gojovic, do you mind that document being photocopied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly don't mind. On the contrary, I would be glad. But I think it has been photocopied and submitted to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And if -- if it can be made available by the witness to whoever is doing the photocopying. You see -- immediately at the close of the hearing today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, if we can go back to where we were on pages 76 and -- 80 -- 68, 68 for you, there's an important fact about Izbica, isn't there, General Gojovic, that we should have in mind; namely that this was the mass burial site that was subject of a video produced by the United States at a very early date in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 162 tab 7, for reference of the Court, and tab 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular killing site was publicised internationally, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was publicised internationally. I didn't follow that. But I do know that the international public opinion was informed and focused on that quite a lot. But this is not a case of a mass grave. It is a series of individual graves in a small area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see -- well, whatever. We've got evidence that the United States briefed in respect of Izbica at an early date in, it appears, March of 1999, that there was an aerial photograph taken of a gravesite outside Izbica in May of 1999, and my inquiry of you is this: Is the reason that Izbica is the only serious crime charged in this indictment that finds a reflection in your schedule, that with the international attention focused on it there was no way you could ignore it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing: In our overview, we have another case of this kind involving 140 graves of victims. In another case yet, 175, that those cases were developed and processed. So there can be no question of what you are saying. What the American services made aerial photographs of cannot be the decisive factor in taking on a case or not. Look at this case of Dosevac. 140 bodies. Ninety-five in Senovac. What's the difference between 95 or 140 compared to 120 that you quoted in the indictment? You cannot take the fact that the American services made a photograph of something as a very important factor. An incident that is not accompanied by a record of investigative organs cannot go anywhere. It doesn't matter what American services recorded. It's what the judiciary and the police discover that matters to us in deciding whether we are going to go ahead with a case or not. The public opinion, international public opinion included does not matter, has no importance, is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The evidence we have, which is Exhibit 162, tab 7, from the United States has the matter recorded as there being no graves on the 15th of March and new graves by the 15th of April. From your answers, General Gojovic, are you saying that public -- international public opinion or international public broadcasting of allegations about what had happened did play a part in the decision whether to investigate?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was publicised internationally or not is something that the judiciary organs were not aware of. They were not even a position to follow the international press or television. The prosecutor had the obligation to report it and start a case. What American TV stations reported on doesn't matter. They reported on things that never happened, in some cases. As for when these bodies were buried, it doesn't mean anything. They could have been buried before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military prosecutors and military court judges have a freestanding duty to investigate -- to inquire into and to investigate matters that may concern the military, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you've told us, you're independent of politics.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you investigate Racak, given the broad public allegations about the involvement of forces included the army? Why didn't you investigate it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor did not have the evidence to start the case. What the public says are only stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... only stories. Tell me, how do investigations start if they don't start with stories? This is a very serious event at Racak. Why did the military judicial system of the country in which it happened - and Serbia's been very proud of its integration at the time with Kosovo or the other way around - why didn't it investigate Racak?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't investigate Racak if they had no evidence that a single soldier killed anyone there or that a military unit attacked Racak population centre. Why would then the military prosecutor investigate that incident if the investigative judge of the district court in Pristina went to the sight to investigate accompanied by the police and the relatives of the victims? I don't know what piece of evidence constitutes grounds for you to link the military prosecutor to this event. There is no such piece of evidence. What Walker said on the scene, the statements he made and the stories that circulated in the public, that doesn't matter at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you haven't attended to the evidence of people like Maisonneuve who were quite specific in seeing tanks firing into Racak. You've never focused on that yourself.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few other things. I'll have to come back to tabs 17 and 18 after the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this was a document that wasn't listed under the 65 ter, nor was it supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal with this quite shortly, the next point, although it might be necessary to look at some documents.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, Mr. President. With regard to tab 18, if you allow me one explanation after this remark made by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
